title: Borrowing a login
topic: Probity in records, forms and certification
stem:
You are an F2 doctor on a respiratory ward. Your colleague Dr Okoro, another F2, has been locked out of the hospital computer system. He needs to request an urgent CT pulmonary angiogram for a patient he has just assessed.

He asks to use your login, saying, "It'll only take a minute, and it's for the patient."
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.brief: Requests are recorded under the logged-in user.
options.detailed: The system records the request as yours, so you would be accountable for a clinical decision you didn't make. Sharing logins also breaches information governance rules.

options.text: Log in for him and let him make the request.
options.brief: The request would still appear as yours.
options.detailed: This is the same as sharing your login: the record would show you made a request you didn't make.

options.text: Ask a nurse to request the scan.
options.brief: Nurses usually can't request this kind of scan.
options.detailed: Requests for a CT pulmonary angiogram generally need a doctor, and this passes the problem to someone else.

options.text: Request the scan yourself, once you've discussed the patient.
options.brief: Gets the urgent scan requested properly.
options.detailed: If you understand the clinical reasoning and agree, you can make the request under your own name and take responsibility for it. This keeps the record accurate and avoids delay.

options.text: Tell him to leave the request until his account has been unlocked.
options.detailed: A suspected pulmonary embolism needs prompt imaging. Waiting could harm the patient.

options.text: Suggest he contacts the IT helpdesk to unlock his account.
options.detailed: He will need access for the rest of his shift. Getting his account unlocked quickly fixes the problem.

options.text: Share your login this once, as it's urgent.
options.brief: Urgency doesn't justify breaching security rules.
options.detailed: There is a safe alternative: requesting it yourself. Sharing your login is unnecessary.

options.text: Write a paper request with his name and your signature.
options.brief: Mixes up who is responsible for the request.
options.detailed: This creates confusion about who requested the scan and doesn't follow the usual process.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you keep to information governance rules under time pressure, while still getting the patient the care they need.
explanation.keyDetails: The scan is urgent. His account is locked. Sharing logins breaches rules. You can request it yourself.
explanation.reasoning: [A] protects the integrity of the record, [D] gets the scan requested properly, and [F] fixes his access. The distractors share access in effect ([B], [G]), pass on the problem ([C]), delay ([E]), or confuse responsibility ([H]).
explanation.competing: [G] is tempting because it is urgent. But requesting it yourself is just as quick and doesn't breach the rules.
